title: Langar on the highway
hookLine: in the farmers' protests of 2020 and 2021 langar fed protesters on the roads

cards: Tractors parked nose to tail along a highway, as far down the road as the eye can follow. Behind them, steam rising from huge pots. Somebody kneading dough on a tarp.
Somebody flipping rotis on a wide iron griddle. A row of people sitting on the asphalt, plates in their laps.

Farmers had come to the edges of Delhi to protest new farm laws, and they camped there, on the roads, through heat and through cold. A camp that size needs feeding. Nobody set up a canteen with a cash register.

teach.b: First, the camp. People held different views about the farm laws, and this lesson isn't here to settle that. It's here for the kitchen.
Among the farmers on the roads were Sikhs from Punjab, and they brought what Sikhs bring when a crowd gathers: rations, cooks, and the habit of feeding anyone who sits down. Second, the root.
Langar is the free kitchen of the Guru's house, and Sikh tradition traces it back to the Gurus themselves.

teach.h: ANG 967: STORES THAT NEVER RUN SHORT.
teach.b: In a hymn by the bards Satta and Balwand, at Ang 967 of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru's langar runs on, and its stores never run short.
The same hymn praises Mata Khivi, the wife of Guru Angad, who served in the langar, giving out rich rice pudding made with ghee, and whose kindness gave wide shade.
From the start, langar was a kitchen with names and hands. Third, the road. On the highway, langar did what it does in a gurdwara: it didn't check who you were.
Farmers ate, and so did passersby, reporters, and people who simply lived nearby and walked over. Volunteers washed dishes on the roadside; some kept pots going through the night. Fourth, the point.
A gurdwara is a building, but langar was never really about the building. It's a habit: where people gather, cook; where people are tired, feed them; and sit together, in a row, on the same ground.
When the farmers moved onto the road, the kitchen didn't wait for them to come back.

how: Sikhs serve langar, a free communal meal, at gurdwaras, and volunteers often take it out to where people gather, at protests, disasters and long journeys.

o: the Guru's free kitchen, open to anyone
a meal Sikhs eat only on festival days
a canteen that sells food at a low price

games.q: the kitchen on the road — tap the pairs.
p: served rice pudding made with ghee

s: on the highway, langar fed only the farmers
it fed whoever sat down: farmers, passersby, reporters, neighbors.
the Guru Granth Sahib praises a woman who served in the langar
Satta and Balwand's hymn at Ang 967 praises Mata Khivi.
langar needs a gurdwara building to happen
it's a habit, not a building: where people gather, the kitchen comes along.

games.q: you're a farmer camped on a highway with a crowd that needs feeding. what do you set up?
o: a stall that sells food at cost.
a langar that feeds anyone who sits down.
games.why: they set up langar on the road, and it fed passersby and neighbors as well as the farmers.

practice: Bring to mind one person who is worn out right now, a parent on night shifts, a friend in a hard month, a coworker carrying too much, and see their face.
On a breath out, ask one plain question, what could I bring them to eat or drink, and let one answer arrive without planning the whole thing. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Langar. The Guru's free kitchen, which went with farmers camped on the highway and fed whoever sat down. Today's word.
